language.script_notes: French is dominant and often exclusive on signage in Quebec; English dominant in Ontario and the Maritimes, with French appearing bilingually via federal signage.
false_friends: Northeastern US (similar architecture near the border)

road_furniture.bollard_color: Quebec: long, thin white posts always attached to guardrails, with a red or green reflector at the top — a strong, reliable Quebec-specific tell, sometimes paired with yellow fire-hydrant markers on signposts (Quebec City's often carry a blue rectangle). Ontario: diamond-shaped roadside markers that vary in colour.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Varies by province as described above.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Quebec's bollard-on-guardrail combination as a specific regional tell.
road_furniture.curb_style: Dense formal infrastructure in Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Ontario's speed-limit signs explicitly include a 'km/h' label in white text on black at the bottom.

architecture.roof_style: The Ontario Style House (rectangular wood-frame with a gable over the short side, a smaller entrance gable) is a distinctive historic Ontario form; Quebec's French Catholic churches use a distinct architectural tradition that did not adopt the High Gothic Revival style common in Ontario/Maritime churches.
architecture.wall_construction: Quebec's older towns carry a distinct French-Canadian architectural character (steep silver tin roofs, dormer windows); Maritime coastal towns feature lighthouses and clapboard fishing-village architecture.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Muted wood-frame tones nationally; Quebec's older buildings sometimes carry French colonial-era grey stone.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Quebec's French Catholic churches and old-town architecture (Quebec City, Old Montreal); Ontario-style historic wood-frame farmhouses; Maritime lighthouses and clapboard fishing villages; Toronto's modern skyline.

nature.vegetation: Dense mixed and boreal forest across most of the region; the Canadian Shield's lake-and-forest terrain covers much of Ontario/Quebec; a rugged Atlantic coastline in the Maritimes (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI, Newfoundland).
nature.terrain: The Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River valley form the demographic core; the Canadian Shield's rock, forest and lakes dominate further north; the Maritime provinces sit on a rugged Atlantic coast.
nature.climate_signature: Cold snowy winters, warm humid summers; vivid autumn foliage; coastal fog and maritime climate in the Atlantic provinces.

vehicles.plate_color: Ontario white-with-blue-text ('Yours to Discover'), Quebec blue-on-white with a fleur-de-lis, Maritime provinces embossed red (New Brunswick) or blue (Nova Scotia) on white.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Heaviest overall vehicle density given this region holds most of Canada's population.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Best and most current coverage in the country, concentrated around Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and the Maritime coastal towns.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Very dense, near-complete coverage — most 'generic Canada' Street View imagery comes from this region.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Same country, same plate/bollard base style
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Eastern Canada is forested/lake-covered with dense population centers; the Prairies are flat farmland, the West is mountainous, and the North is Arctic tundra — all visually distinct.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared French language in Quebec, some similar Catholic church architectural roots
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Quebec's road furniture (guardrail-mounted bollards, km/h signage, North American plate format) is distinctly Canadian, and the surrounding wood-frame architecture looks nothing like rural France.
